verdicts.reason: Identifies the proposed Sackler release as running in favor of the Sackler family and related nondebtor entities.
Distinguishes estate-owned fraudulent-transfer claims from victims’ direct opioid claims against the Sacklers.
States the release could not be imposed on non-consenting opioid claimants and describes compelled extinguishment without consent.
Repeatedly treats the Sacklers as nondebtors/third parties receiving protection, not as debtors obtaining their own discharges.
Explains the Sacklers’ proposed contribution was in exchange for extinguishing estate claims and ending opioid litigation, and notes it was a proposal.
Contrasts low eligible-creditor participation and thousands of opposing victims with majority support among returned ballots.
Recounts bankruptcy-court confirmation, district-court vacatur, Second Circuit revival, and Supreme Court reversal.
Uses the respondent brief as plan-proponent advocacy, not as binding law, while correctly identifying its arguments.
States § 105(a) only carries out authority conferred elsewhere and does not independently authorize the release.
Identifies § 1123(b)(6) as the disputed catchall for “any other appropriate provision.”
Explains the majority’s ejusdem generis reading of the catchall in light of the debtor-related paragraphs (1)–(5).
Separates settlement of estate-owned claims under § 1123(b)(3) from extinguishment of creditors’ direct claims against nondebtors.
Explains that labeling the relief a “release” rather than a “discharge” did not avoid discharge limits.
Connects the holding to ordinary discharge limitations, including fraud, willful-injury, wrongful-death claims, and failure to place full assets on the table.
Explains the majority rejected the contribution/public-interest policy arguments as a basis for statutory authority and left policy choices to Congress.
Identifies § 524(g) as the specific asbestos exception and says it does not support a general mass-tort authority under § 1123(b)(6).
States the Supreme Court reversed the Second Circuit and remanded.
States the decision does not call consensual third-party releases into question.
States the Court did not define what qualifies as a consensual release.
Identifies the reservation for plans providing full satisfaction of claims against a third-party nondebtor.
Identifies the reservation concerning plans already effective and substantially consummated.
Frames the decision as a statutory-authority holding and does not report any Supreme Court damages verdict on the opioid claims.
States remand leaves further proceedings and unresolved plan confirmation and negotiation issues.
Limits the holding to the challenged nonconsensual nondebtor release and injunction, not all third-party injunctions.
Fairly presents the dissent’s practical argument that individual litigation could destroy collective recovery and the settlement fund.
Labels the dissent and plan-proponent positions as separate advocacy, not the governing majority rule.
Warns that removing the release may cause the Sacklers to contribute less or not at all, affecting recoveries, without inventing a new guaranteed amount.
Considers a genuinely consensual release while flagging the unsettled meaning of consent.
Considers preserving estate-owned claim settlements while leaving direct claims against the Sacklers outstanding.
The update distinguishes claim ownership and lists claimant groups, but it does not expressly request an identification of claim owners and release beneficiaries before revising scope.
Flags that the consent mechanism, affected claimant populations, future claimants, and representative consent must be addressed before revising the release.
Identifies the need to confirm whether the Sacklers will continue funding and on what revised settlement terms after remand.
